_README: List prices and billing rules for the VM types a batch tile can land on,
read by landsat_lst.pricing to turn a measured wall clock into dollars.
This file is data, so a price change is an edit here rather than a code
change. Update as_of whenever a rate moves, because a stale rate that
reads as current is the failure this file exists to avoid.
on_demand_usd_hour, memory_gib, vcpu and the billing minimum are published
by the vendor, so they carry provenance 'published'. A tile cost built
from them and a measured duration is 'derived'. Only the spot band is
'assumed', and it is the reason a spot cost is an interval.
Both entries of settings.coiled_vm_types carry 64 GiB, which is why
profiling.DEFAULT_VM_GIB is a single 64.0 rather than a lookup. The other
two rows exist to price history, not to be scheduled: r6i.4xlarge is the
VM every figure in calibration.json was measured on, and r6i.xlarge is the
32 GiB machine that OOMed a heavy tile at 28.77 GiB.
Regions are not interchangeable and are not interpolated. A region absent
from this table has no price here, and the caller reports that rather than

billing.note: EC2 Linux bills per second with a 60 second minimum per instance launch. A task that ran 10.375 seconds and died still billed a full minute, which is why short failures are not free.

spot_band.note: Spot is priced per instance type, per availability zone, per minute, and a finished run cannot be repriced against the rate it actually paid. Nothing this pipeline publishes records it. So a spot cost is an interval spanning the observed spread, not a scalar. The samples below were quoted on one day in one region across one instance generation and still ranged from 0.35 to 0.71 of on-demand, so a single factor would be wrong by more than 2x for one of the two configured VM types.

r6i.xlarge.note: Not scheduled. Kept to price the run that OOMed at 28.77 GiB.

r6i.4xlarge.note: Not scheduled. Kept to price run 2021-2025-sample300-20260813T123249Z and every other calibration.json record.
